newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: HORSE RACING Feature-Irish racing industry to get a boost.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING Feature-Irish racing industry to get a boost.

text.p: Irish horses race first past the post around the world. But at home racing is only just turning the corner after running a distant third for years in appeal behind television and soccer.

Falling attendances at down-at-heel race tracks and a drop in on-course betting have combined to force a re-think in an industry which is as Irish as Guinness or county Kildare, home of the coveted Irish bloodstock industry.
Racing authorities say the sport is on the mend and that radical new plans to inject cash, the lifeblood of any sport, should help give Irish horses the setting they deserve.
Last year was one of growth for the sport with an eight percent rise in attendance, a 13 percent increase in on-course betting turnover and a six percent jump in prize money.

"They are not staggering increases but certainly they are very positive. They represent an improvement over recent years and hopefully we have now turned the corner," Noel Ryan, Chief Executive of the Irish Horseracing Authority, said in an interview.
The IHA said in its review of racing for 1996 that 1.1 million people attended 258 racing fixtures at Ireland's 25 racecourses in 1996.
It said the aim was to increase annual attendances by 200,000 paying customers to 1.3 million by the year 2001 and that its main target area would be the younger generation.

This stay-at-home section of the community shuns race tracks, which cannot compete with sport on British television beamed in by satellite television, or offer the more lavish facilities which are features of race tracks in Britain and France.

IHA chairman Denis Brosnan said the ultimate objective was to create a vibrant racing industry with racecourse facilities at Ireland's major racecourses on a par with the best elsewhere and with all tracks upgraded in standard.
"We need also to increase prize money and sponsorship," Brosnan said. "To enable all these objectives to be achieved, we need to put the funding of the industry on a sound footing."
To this end, the IHA said it would radically transform the Tote, a cash and credit betting service on-course and an off-course credit betting service.

"The Tote has the potential to bridge the gap between the finance currently available to the industry, which is adequate, and the level of finance that it so desperately needs," Brosnan said in an interview.
"We have set ourselves an ambitious target in relation to the Tote but we believe that it is realistic and attainable."

The IHA said if the right steps were taken to reduce the cost of operating the Tote, with a turnover of 34.3 million punts ($54.6 million) by the year 2001, an overall net contribution of 2.5 million punts ($4 million) would accrue to racing.
"The capital cost of bringing this about will be substantial both in terms of restructuring (staff-related costs) and investment in technology and equipment," he said.
"After the pay-back period, racing will have available a substantial new source of income to improve prize-money and develop the industry more fully."
One industry in which the Irish continue to show the way is bloodstock. Ireland exports horses to around 40 countries.
No part of the world is ignored by the IHA, which is responsible for running the industry in Ireland, seeking to find homes for the 6,500 foals born at Irish studs every year.
"Over the last two years, our two biggest new markets would have to be (South) Korea and China," IHA Marketing Director Matt Mitchell said.
"160 Irish thoroughbreds were exported to Korea for breeding and training purposes over the last two years while nine were exported to China."
Mitchell said the fact that Irish-bred horses constantly score big wins on the international racing circuit boosted the reputation of Ireland's bloodstock industry.
Jodami, winner of the 1993 Cheltenham Gold Cup, and Mark of Esteem, the 1996 English 2,000 Guineas winner, are two of the best known Irish-bred racehorses.
"The fact that the soil and climate here is suited to breeding and racing and that there is a stallion income tax exemption in Ireland has also helped boost the industry," Mitchell said.
One fifth of the 25,000 earning an income, including those employed in related industries, from Irish racing are employed in bloodstock.

As a result of the Stallion Income Tax Exemption introduced in 1969, Irish breeding has thrived with some of the leading stallions in the world, including Sadler's Wells and College Chapel, standing at studs in Ireland.
The measures waives income tax on Irish blodstock breeders with the aim of ploughing their profits back into the industry while the offspring fly the Irish flag on foreign fields.
